docs.title: 📘 Introduction
docs.text:
Welcome to the TerraBrasilis Airflow Guide — the official documentation designed to support the development and maintenance of Airflow tasks within the TerraBrasilis project.

This guide provides examples, explanations, and best practices for creating Airflow tasks in a standardized and efficient way. Our goal is to ensure consistency, readability, and maintainability across all workflows.

docs.title: 🎯 Purpose
docs.text:
The primary objective of this documentation is to:

  • Define best practices for writing and organizing Airflow tasks (DAGs and operators).
  • Encourage a standardized structure for all DAGs to facilitate collaboration and ease onboarding for new developers.
  • Improve maintainability and debuggability of tasks through clear conventions and naming patterns.
  • Promote reusability and modularity to reduce code duplication and improve overall system reliability.
  • Ensure all tasks are aligned with the TerraBrasilis project architecture and objectives.

docs.title: 📌 Who Is This For?
docs.text:
This guide is intended for:

  • Developers contributing to TerraBrasilis pipelines using Apache Airflow.
  • New team members who need a consistent reference to understand and extend the system.

docs.title: 🛠️ What You'll Find Here
docs.text:
Inside this documentation, you'll find:

  • Guidelines on naming conventions, folder structure, and task documentation.
  • Examples of well-structured DAGs and custom operators.
  • Tips for scheduling, dependency management, and error handling.
  • Instructions for logging, monitoring, and alerting in Airflow.
  • Version control and deployment recommendations.

docs.title: 🧭 Get Started
docs.text:
To begin, head over to the Best Practices section or explore the sidebar for specific topics of interest.

Let’s build reliable, consistent, and maintainable data workflows — together.

docs.title: Best Practices for Airflow Tasks
docs.text: This section outlines the recommended best practices for designing and developing Airflow DAGs and tasks within the TerraBrasilis project. Following these guidelines ensures a consistent, maintainable, and scalable workflow structure.

docs.title: 🧮 Airflow Variables
docs.text: Airflow Variables are useful for storing configuration values and secrets that might change between environments or deployments. To ensure consistency and clarity across all DAGs, the following conventions must be followed.

docs.title: 📚 Managing Variables via the UI
docs.text:
To add or edit variables via the Airflow web UI:

  1. Navigate to Admin > Variables.
  2. Click Create to add a new variable.
  3. Enter the Key (name), and the Value (string or JSON).
  4. Fill in the Description field with a brief explanation of the variable’s purpose.
  5. Click Save.

docs.title: 🔧 Accessing Variables
docs.text:
You can access Airflow variables using the Variable class:

from airflow.models import Variable

# Access a variable
value = Variable.get("MY_VARIABLE_NAME")

# Access a variable with a default value
value = Variable.get("MY_VARIABLE_NAME", default_var="default_value")

# Access and parse a JSON-formatted variable
config = Variable.get("MY_JSON_VARIABLE", deserialize_json=True)

docs.title: 📌 Naming Conventions
docs.text:
All Airflow variables must follow these naming rules:

  • ✅ Use English for all variable names.
  • ✅ Use UPPERCASE letters only.
  • ✅ Use underscores (_) to separate words.
  • ✅ Always include a reference to the DAG name or acronym as a prefix, to indicate where the variable is used.
  • ✅ Always fill in the Description field with a brief explanation of the variable's purpose and where it is used.

docs.title: ✅ Good Examples
docs.text: Variable Name Description RISKDB_CMASK_SATELLITES Used in the riskdb DAG to configure satellite list PRODES_EXPORT_FOLDER_PATH Used in the prodes DAG to define export folder DEFORESTATION_API_TOKEN Token used by deforestation DAG

docs.title: ❌ Bad Examples (to avoid)
docs.text: Variable Name Issue satelliteList Not uppercase, not in English list_sat No reference to DAG prodespath Unclear meaning, not readable

docs.title: 🧼 Tips for Using Variables
docs.text:
• Prefer Airflow Connections or secrets backends for sensitive information like passwords or tokens.
  • Keep variables centralized and consistent across environments. You can use the Import/Export JSON feature in the UI.

docs.title: 🔗 Airflow Connections
docs.text: Airflow Connections are used to securely store credentials and connection details (such as host, port, username, password, API tokens) for external systems. They help avoid hardcoding sensitive data directly in DAGs or code.

docs.title: 🔧 Accessing Connections
docs.text:
To view and manage Connections in the Airflow Web UI:

  1. Go to Admin > Connections.
  2. Here you will see a list of existing connections.
  3. Click Create to add a new connection or click on an existing one to edit it.
  4. Fill in the required fields: Conn Id, Conn Type, Host, Login, Password, Port, Schema, and Extra.
  5. Fill in the Description field with a brief explanation of the connection’s purpose.
  6. Click Save.

docs.title: 📌 Naming Conventions
docs.text:
All Airflow connections must follow these naming rules:

  • ✅ Use English for all connection IDs (Conn Id).
  • ✅ Use UPPERCASE letters only.
  • ✅ Use underscores (_) to separate words.
  • ✅ Always include a reference to the DAG name or acronym as a prefix to indicate where the connection is used.
  • ✅ Always fill in the Description field explaining the connection’s purpose and where it is used.

docs.title: ✅ Good Examples
docs.text: Conn Id Description RISKDB_POSTGRES Postgres database connection for riskdb DAG PRODES_S3_BUCKET AWS S3 bucket connection used by prodes DAG DEFORESTATION_API_SERVICE API service connection for deforestation DAG

docs.title: ❌ Bad Examples (to avoid)
docs.text: Conn Id Issue postgres No DAG reference, too generic s3bucket Not uppercase, no underscores deforestationapi No separators, unclear meaning (no description) Missing description reduces clarity

docs.title: 🧼 Tips for Managing Connections
docs.text:
• Avoid hardcoding credentials in DAGs or variables; use Connections instead.
  • Use the Extra field to store JSON-formatted parameters when needed.
  • Keep connections centralized and documented with clear descriptions.
  • Use different connections for different environments (dev, staging, prod) with consistent naming prefixes.
  • Regularly audit connections to remove unused or expired credentials.

docs.title: 📝 What is PEP8?
docs.text: PEP8 is the Python Enhancement Proposal 8, which defines the official style guide for writing Python code. It provides a set of conventions and best practices to make Python code more readable, consistent, and maintainable across projects and teams.

docs.title: ❓ Why Use PEP8?
docs.text:
• 👀 Improves readability: Code that follows a consistent style is easier to read and understand.
  • 🤝 Enhances maintainability: Uniform code style helps teams collaborate and maintain projects more efficiently.
  • 🛡️ Reduces errors: Clear formatting helps prevent bugs caused by confusing or unclear code structure.
  • ⭐ Promotes best practices: Following widely accepted standards ensures code quality and professional development habits.

docs.title: ⚙️ How to Use PEP8?
docs.text:
• Follow the naming conventions, indentation, spacing, and line length rules described in PEP8.
  • Use tools like flake8, pylint, or black to automatically check and format your code.
  • Review PEP8 guidelines regularly to improve code style.

You can read the official PEP8 document here: https://peps.python.org/pep-0008/

docs.title: 1. 🔤 Variable Naming
docs.text:
• Use lowercase words separated by underscores (snake_case).
  • Avoid single character names except for counters or iterators.
user_name = "John"
total_amount = 100
counter = 0

docs.title: 2. ⚙️ Function Naming
docs.text:
• Use lowercase words separated by underscores (snake_case).
  • Function names should be descriptive of their purpose.
def calculate_total(price, tax_rate):
    total = price + price * tax_rate
    return total

docs.title: 3. 🏷️ Class Naming
docs.text:
• Use CapWords (also called PascalCase or CamelCase) convention.
  • Class names should be nouns and describe the object.
class UserProfile:
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age

docs.title: 4. ↪️ Indentation and Spacing
docs.text:
• Use 4 spaces per indentation level.
  • Limit lines to a maximum of 79 characters.
  • Surround top-level functions and classes with two blank lines.
  • Use one blank line inside functions to separate logical sections.
def greet_user(name):
    if name:
        print(f"Hello, {name}!")
    else:
        print("Hello, Guest!")

docs.title: 📌 Summary
docs.text: Following PEP8 is a standard way to write clean, readable, and professional Python code. It makes your code easier for others (and yourself) to read, understand, and maintain.

docs.title: Using PythonVirtualenvOperator in TerraBrasilis Airflow DAGs
docs.text: The PythonVirtualenvOperator is useful when your Airflow task requires specific Python dependencies that may not be available in the main Airflow environment. It allows you to run a Python function in a virtual environment, isolated from the system packages.

docs.title: 📥 Importing the Operator
docs.text:
First, make sure to import the operator using:

from airflow.operators.python import PythonVirtualenvOperator

docs.title: 1. Define the Path in Your DAG
docs.text:
In your DAG file, define the path to your virtualenv, you don't need to create it in your environment beforehand, as Airflow will automatically handle its creation during execution.:

venv_path = "/opt/airflow/venv/inpe/pantanal_deter_cmask_data_flow/venv"

docs.title: 2. Difine the requirements
docs.text:
It is necessary to store all the parameters required for the DAG execution in a local variable, so that Airflow can properly install the dependencies during execution.

requirements = [
    "requests",
    "psycopg2-binary",
    "geopandas==0.13.2",
    "fiona==1.9.6",
    "geoalchemy2",
    "rasterstats",
    "libpysal",
    "beautifulsoup4",
    "rasterio",
    "apache-airflow==2.10.5"
]

docs.title: 3. Use the PythonVirtualenvOperator in Tasks
docs.text:
You can now create tasks using the operator. In the first call to the PythonVirtualenvOperator, you need to provide the requirements parameter so that Airflow can install the previously defined packages:

task_1 = PythonVirtualenvOperator(
    task_id="1_trigger_task",
    requirements=requirements,
    python_callable=task_callable_01,
    system_site_packages=True,
    op_kwargs={"biome": biome},
    venv_cache_path=venv_path
)

In subsequent calls to the PythonVirtualenvOperator, it will no longer be necessary to pass the requirements parameter, as all dependencies will have already been installed in the virtual environment, which will be reused in the following calls.

task_2 = PythonVirtualenvOperator(
    task_id='2_create_tables_task',
    python_callable=task_callable_02,
    system_site_packages=True,
    op_kwargs={"biome": biome},
    venv_cache_path=venv_path
)
  • python_callable: your Python function.
  • op_kwargs: keyword arguments to pass to the function.
  • system_site_packages=True: allows access to system-wide packages if needed.
  • venv_cache_path: the path to your virtual environment.

docs.title: 🔁 Sharing Data with XComs
docs.text: To pass values between tasks using XComs:

docs.title: Return values in your function:
docs.text:
def task_callable_01(biome):
    result = {"satellite": "CBERS", "year": 2024}
    return result

docs.title: Use op_kwargs in dependent tasks:
docs.text:
task_2 = PythonVirtualenvOperator(
    task_id="2_process_result",
    python_callable=task_callable_02,
    op_kwargs={"result": task_1.output},
    venv_cache_path=venv_path
)

docs.title: ✅ Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use a consistent folder structure for virtualenvs inside the /opt/airflow/projects directory.
  • Keep dependencies lean and versioned.
  • Always return structured data (like dictionaries) when using XComs.
